items.abstract: <jats:p>Muslim minorities are documented as taxpayers or legal subjects in medieval Europe, but rarely as individuals or households. This study examines carbon and nitrogen stable isotopes from 120 individuals buried at Torre Monreal, Tudela (Navarre, Spain) between the late eleventh and fifteenth centuries to build a picture of everyday food access in an Islamic community under Christian rule. The results, the authors argue, show a long-term reorganisation of diet that reflects historical narratives on the legal accessibility and market availability of freshwater and terrestrial resources, and are presented here as evidence for adaptive food practices rather than dietary assimilation.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Rice agriculture profoundly shapes the dietary and subsistence patterns of Neolithic populations in the lower Yangtze River region. However, direct evidence regarding human diet and livestock management strategies during the middle Neolithic, the early rice agriculture period, is still lacking. The Kuahuqiao site (8200–7000 BP) provides critical material for addressing this issue. This case study presents stable isotope data derived from bone collagen of one human and 129 animal specimens recovered from the site, offering direct dietary evidence. The results show that wild animals (deer and water buffalo) exhibit a broad range of isotopic values, reflecting diverse dietary resources and implying the existence of complex foraging environments and ecological conditions. Domestic dogs show isotopic values close to those of the individual, with no clear diachronic trend, indicating that their diets were predominantly C
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    ‐based, most likely derived from human food refuse. Pigs display considerable isotopic variability, particularly in
                    <jats:italic>δ</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>15</jats:sup>
                    N values. In conjunction with zooarchaeological evidence, this study attributes the wide range primarily to the coexistence of domestic and wild pigs, together with the consumption of human food refuse or faeces by domestic pigs. Moreover, diachronic isotopic and zooarchaeological data collectively point to a trend of intensified management of domestic pigs at the site. The single individual predominantly consumed substantial amounts of C
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    ‐based foods, including C
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    plants such as rice and wild animals such as deer, with a possible supplementary contribution from freshwater resources. These findings suggest that the Kuahuqiao inhabitants established an early agricultural system that integrated rice cultivation, livestock husbandry and hunting‐fishing‐gathering activities, resulting in a diversified subsistence strategy centred on rice farming. This study provides early direct isotopic evidence for human dietary patterns and livestock management strategies during the middle Neolithic in the lower Yangtze River region and represents a large‐scale isotopic study for this region to date.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The Moroccan coast provides valuable insight into how large‐scale climate and sea‐level variations have manifested themselves at the regional level. In this paper, we present new findings from shallow marine deposits in the Achakkar Basin near Tangier, Morocco. Data from these deposits record approximately 10 kyr of sea‐level highstand during the Last Interglacial period, deduced from a multidisciplinary study integrating sedimentological, micropalaeontological, palynological and ichnological records. Three facies associations are distinguished in the studied section. The lowest association is interpreted as deposits of migrating subtidal sand dune. The intermediate facies association reflects lower energy conditions in a more distal tempestite lower shoreface setting. The uppermost coarse‐grained interval indicates the transition to an upper shoreface to foreshore zone characterized by significantly increased energy. In addition, the micropalaeontological study shows an abundance of benthic foraminifera. The dominance of benthic forms suggests that the sedimentary environment was dominated by conditions suitable for the establishment of shallow‐water fauna, such as those found in shoreface environments. Species such as
                    <jats:italic>Ammonia beccarii</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>Elphidium crispum</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Nonion faba</jats:italic>
                    , which are widespread in the lower levels of the sequence, are known for their increased ecological tolerance and ability to survive in unstable, low‐salinity environments. Furthermore, palynological and ichnological evidence supports the micropalaeontological and sedimentological findings, indicating a transition from nearshore to more distal environments, followed by a return to unstable, high‐energy nearshore conditions. These integrated data provide a significant contribution to the understanding of palaeoenvironmental studies within climate‐sensitive nearshore sediments.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advances in postmortem imaging technologies are transforming medical examiner practice, enabling the creation of large‐scale digital collections of decedent data that support research across medicine, public health, forensics, bioarchaeology, paleoanthropology, demographics, and anthropology in general. Drawing on the case of the New Mexico Decedent Image Database (NMDID), this paper explores the promises and risks of virtual medicolegal collections, introduces the perspectives of next‐of‐kin from a pilot focus group, and confronts the gaps in existing professional and legal frameworks. Finally, this work attempts to establish a foundation for developing standards for ethical stewardship of digital remains in the modern medicolegal landscape.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      One pilot focus group (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 5) was conducted in Kalamazoo, Michigan in 2022. De‐identified transcripts underwent a thematic analysis by anthropologists, ethicists, and biomedical informaticians. Themes were determined when the majority of the focus group agreed or shared the same or similar statement.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From the small group of five participants, seven unique themes were identified relating to the use of decedent data, from the conversations with NOK: legitimate identifiability, closure, advocacy, legitimacy of research, timing of inquiry, notification, and agency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Despite not obtaining saturation due to small group size, the thematic analysis still provides an important stakeholder perspective to help identify key aspects of the history and legal context of the unique ethical challenges posed by using medical examiner imaging‐based collections for research purposes. Building on this foundation, we propose eight
                      <jats:italic>preliminary</jats:italic>
                      ethical guidelines that emphasize confidentiality, security, stewardship, and respect for next‐of‐kin.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Kori Mecklenburg, Christine Pink, Heather J. H. Edgar, Tyler S. Gibb, Philip J. Kroth, Shamsi Daneshvari Berry

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>While several marine and terrestrial sediment records provide the general climate boundary conditions for Iberia at a relatively low temporal resolution (often >100 years per sample) during the last several glacial cycles, few high‐resolution proxy records of continental climate have been developed from this region. Speleothems can provide millennia of seasonally to decadally resolved data on vegetation dynamics and hydroclimate variability. In this study we use stable carbon and oxygen isotopes and magnesium concentrations from a stalagmite collected from a cave in southern Portugal to better understand environmental variability during part of marine isotope stage (MIS) 4: ~69–64 ka. Stalagmite growth ceased as temperatures decreased just prior to the start of Heinrich stadial 6, an exceptionally cold period in the North Atlantic region, and growth did not resume after Heinrich event 6, suggesting dry and/or cold conditions in southern Portugal. Integration of these new data with previously published proxy records in western Europe reveals a complex and heterogenous spatial pattern of hydroclimate variability during MIS 4. For example, some regional stalagmite records, including those in Iberia, continued growing during Heinrich stadial 6, suggesting that a fine‐scale heterogeneity in precipitation patterns existed, or that infiltration pathways in these caves remained intact.</jats:p>
